title: Urinary tract infection (adult): cystitis, pyelonephritis, complicated and catheter UTI
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Treat afebrile cystitis with nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin. For complicated UTI (fever, flank pain, systemic signs) culture first, choose empirical therapy by sepsis status, prior cultures and local resistance, switch to oral when improving and stop at 7 days in most. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

sections.title: Classify (IDSA 2025)
items: Uncomplicated UTI (cystitis): dysuria, urgency, frequency or suprapubic pain with no fever, rigors, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness or haemodynamic instability. It can occur in men, diabetics and immunocompromised patients.

Complicated UTI: infection beyond the bladder, suggested by fever, chills, rigors, haemodynamic instability, flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness. Pyelonephritis and symptomatic catheter-associated UTI are complicated UTI.

Catheter-associated UTI: new fever, rigors, flank pain, acute haematuria, pelvic discomfort or unexplained delirium with no other source in a catheterised patient. Cloudy or smelly urine alone is not an indication for antibiotics.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria: a positive urine culture without urinary or systemic symptoms. Screen and treat only in pregnancy and before endoscopic urological procedures that breach the mucosa (IDSA 2019).
Men with febrile UTI may have acute bacterial prostatitis (perineal pain, tender prostate, retention), which needs a longer course.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Typical cystitis in a non-pregnant woman: culture is not needed. Send urine culture for men, pregnancy, recurrence, treatment failure and every complicated UTI.
Complicated UTI: midstream urine culture before antibiotics; blood cultures if febrile or septic; CBC, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose.

Catheterised patient: if the catheter has been in place for more than 2 weeks and is still needed, replace it and culture urine from the new catheter before antibiotics. Never sample from the drainage bag.

Urgent ultrasound of kidneys and bladder in sepsis, AKI, known stones, or no response after 48 to 72 hours, to find obstruction or abscess. CT for suspected emphysematous pyelonephritis, especially in diabetes.
Review urine cultures from the past 3 to 6 months and fluoroquinolone exposure in the past 12 months: both guide the empirical choice.

sections.title: Uncomplicated cystitis
items: First line (ICMR 2022, IDSA): nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days, or fosfomycin trometamol 3 g orally as a single dose.
Co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily for 3 days only if the isolate is susceptible or local E. coli resistance is below 20%; resistance in India is usually higher.
Keep fluoroquinolones for complicated infection; do not use them for simple cystitis.
Men with afebrile cystitis: a 7-day course is commonly used; reassess for prostatitis if fever develops.
Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are for bladder infection only: they do not reach adequate kidney or blood levels.

sections.title: Complicated UTI and pyelonephritis
items: Sepsis: within 1 hour give a third or fourth generation cephalosporin, piperacillin-tazobactam, a carbapenem or a fluoroquinolone, chosen by prior urine cultures, recent fluoroquinolone use and the local antibiogram (at least 90% susceptible in septic shock, 80% in sepsis).
No sepsis: a third or fourth generation cephalosporin, piperacillin-tazobactam or a fluoroquinolone rather than a carbapenem (IDSA 2025).

India (ICMR 2022, high ESBL rates): piperacillin-tazobactam or ertapenem for acute pyelonephritis; imipenem, meropenem or amikacin as alternatives. Use a carbapenem when there is septic shock or a previous ESBL isolate.
Relieve obstruction urgently (percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent) in an infected obstructed kidney; remove or replace an infected urinary catheter.
Narrow to the culture result as soon as it is available.

sections.title: Oral switch and duration
items: Switch to oral when improving, afebrile, able to swallow and an active agent exists: ciprofloxacin 500 to 750 mg twice daily, levofloxacin 750 mg daily, co-trimoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily, or by susceptibility amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg every 8 to 12 hours, cefpodoxime 200 to 400 mg every 12 hours or cefuroxime 500 mg every 12 hours.
Duration if improving (IDSA 2025): fluoroquinolone 5 to 7 days, other agents 7 days, counted from the first day of effective therapy. Gram-negative bacteraemia from a urinary source: 7 days.

Individualise (often 10 to 14 days) for abscess, unrelieved obstruction, slow response or severe immunocompromise. Suspected prostatitis: IDSA suggests 10 to 14 days; ICMR advises at least 21 days for acute prostatitis.
Catheter-associated UTI: 7 days with prompt response, 10 to 14 days with delayed response; remove the catheter if it is no longer needed.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Pregnancy: screen for and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (4 to 7 days) and all cystitis, guided by culture: cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, fosfomycin, or nitrofurantoin (avoid near term). Admit pyelonephritis for IV beta-lactam therapy. Avoid fluoroquinolones.
CKD: adjust all doses to eGFR. Avoid nitrofurantoin below eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 (UK BNF: avoid below 45 except short courses for resistant organisms).
Older adults: do not attribute delirium or falls to a positive dipstick or culture without urinary or systemic signs; look for other causes first.
Diabetes: higher risk of emphysematous pyelonephritis, renal abscess and papillary necrosis; image early if not improving by 48 hours.
Kidney transplant recipients beyond 1 month: do not screen for or treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (IDSA 2019).

sections.title: Escalate
items: Septic shock, AKI, infected obstruction, emphysematous pyelonephritis, or renal or perinephric abscess: urgent urology and critical care input.
No clinical improvement after 48 to 72 hours of active therapy: re-image, recheck culture and susceptibility, and look for an undrained source.
Admit pyelonephritis with vomiting or inability to take oral drugs, pregnancy, significant immunocompromise, or a single functioning kidney.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria or pyuria in catheterised, elderly or diabetic patients.
Using nitrofurantoin or oral fosfomycin for febrile UTI or pyelonephritis.
Empirical ciprofloxacin without local susceptibility data: E. coli fluoroquinolone resistance is high in India.
Treating an obstructed infected kidney with antibiotics alone.

drugs.name: Nitrofurantoin
drugs.dose: 100 mg orally twice daily for 5 days (macrocrystal or modified-release)
drugs.notes: Cystitis only. Avoid at low eGFR and near term in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Fosfomycin trometamol
drugs.dose: 3 g orally as a single dose

drugs.name: Co-trimoxazole (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)
drugs.dose: 160/800 mg orally twice daily: 3 days for cystitis, 7 days for complicated UTI
drugs.notes: Only if susceptible. Monitor potassium and creatinine.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.notes: ICMR first line for pyelonephritis; reduce in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Ertapenem
drugs.notes: ESBL risk without septic shock; no Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter cover.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: Septic shock or known ESBL; renal adjustment.

drugs.name: Amikacin
drugs.notes: ICMR alternative; monitor levels, renal function and hearing; keep courses short.

drugs.name: Ciprofloxacin
drugs.dose: 500 to 750 mg orally twice daily, or 400 mg IV every 12 hours
drugs.notes: Only when susceptible; 5 to 7 day course for complicated UTI.
